data.title: TWSE acts to ease selling pressure
data.description:
TOO MANY UNKNOWNS: Despite policy support, investors must remain vigilant due to near-term market fluidity, Yuanta Securities Investment Consulting Co said

Taiwan Stock Exchange (TWSE) yesterday announced it would lower the minimum margin maintenance ratio to 120 percent from 130 percent to ease forced selling pressure after the TAIEX fell 7,641.83 points, or 17.5 percent, last week to 36,033.29. It was the largest single-week point loss on record and the worst weekly percentage slide in over 35 years.

Because local brokerages need time to update their systems, the adjustment, which aims to reduce the minimum margin requirement for securities financing, takes effect today, the exchange said in a statement.

TWSE said that starting today, brokerages would only issue margin calls if an account’s overall collateral maintenance ratio drops below 120 percent after market close. Investors would have two business days after receiving a notice to cover the shortfall, it said.

In addition, any margin call notices issued before today for accounts whose collateral maintenance ratio fell below 130 percent would be canceled, and brokerages would not liquidate those positions, the exchange said.

Investors can use other collateral that has market liquidity and can be objectively and reasonably evaluated — such as eligible equities or funds — to cover margin shortfalls, subject to their brokerage’s approval, TWSE said.

It also encouraged listed companies to implement stock buyback programs and hold earnings conferences to enhance investor confidence.

TWSE’s move follows a third round of short-selling curbs the Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) announced on Saturday and took effect yesterday, including banning short selling below the previous day’s closing price, raising the minimum short-sale margin requirement to 150 percent from 130 percent, and suspending applications for new put warrants for listing on local bourses.

“With the FSC’s new short-selling curbs and the news about US President Donald Trump’s renewed support for [former CEO] Jensen Huang’s (黃仁勳) return to Nvidia Corp, market confidence has recovered,” Yuanta Securities Investment Consulting Co (元大投顧) said in a note yesterday.

The TAIEX rose 778.6 points, or 2.16 percent, to close at 36,811.89 yesterday as large-cap tech stocks rebounded. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電) rose 1.5 percent, while MediaTek Inc (聯發科) and Delta Electronics Inc (台達電) surged 10 percent each. Several memorychip and printed circuit board stocks also rebounded strongly and hit their daily limit.

Turnover on the local main board expanded to NT$1.079 trillion (US$32.8 billion) from NT$877.35 billion the previous session, TWSE data showed.

The three major institutional investors sold a combined net NT$51.177 billion of local shares, of which foreign investors sold a net NT$28.948 billion, exchange data showed.

Despite policy support, Yuanta said investors must remain vigilant as near-term market development is still fluid, citing factors such as the performance of US tech stocks, Huang’s Senate hearing on Dec. 1, the release of the US personal consumption expenditures index this week and the US Federal Reserve’s potential rate hikes next month.

data.title: TSMC dismisses AI market risks
data.description:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) yesterday dismissed concerns about a deeper correction of the artificial intelligence (AI) market, saying that soaring global demand AI applications continues to outstrip its supply of advanced chips.

The world’s largest contract chipmaker said in a statement that it continues to observe challenges facing the consumer and price-sensitive end-market segments posed by rising component prices and economic uncertainties, TSMC chairman and chief executive officer C.C. Wei’s (魏哲家) remarks during an earnings conference on Oct. 15.

“Global demand for AI continues to grow, with its long-term outlook remaining upbeat,” TSMC said in the statement. “Demand for the company’s leading-edge technologies continues to be extremely robust, supported by our strong technology differentiation and broader customer base.”

TSMC said the long-term trend is creating significant business opportunities for its customers worldwide and unlocking high-value growth potential for the chipmaker.

The value of semiconductors in the global supply chain should increase continuously, TSMC said.

No matter which architecture customers adopt, they would rely on cutting-edge processing technologies, which remain in tight supply, it added.

The output of Taiwan’s semiconductor industry is expected to expand more than 40 percent this year to about NT$9.19 trillion (US$279.4 billion) from NT$6.5 trillion last year, Taiwan Semiconductor Industry Association estimated last month.

TSMC counts Nvidia Corp and the US major cloud service providers, including Amazon.com Inc and Microsoft Corp, among its customers. The chipmaker subscribed a 0.03 percent stake in Anthropic PBC for about US$500 million in the Claude developer’s initial public offering last week.

“All AI players are working with TSMC,” Wei told investors last month. “The gap between demand and supply is still quite big. That’s why we put all our strength into increasing capacity.”

TSMC shares rose 1.5 percent to exceed the key NT$2,000 psychological threshold yesterday, ending a two-day slide, while the broader market gained 2.16 percent after the National Stabilization Fund intervened to steady a market battered by a global AI sell-off.

data.title: Unemployment rate fell to 26-year low last month
data.description:
Taiwan’s unemployment rate fell to a 26-year low last month, while the labor force participation rate climbed to its highest level in nearly 37 years, reflecting growing willingness among women and older people to enter the workforce, the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics (DGBAS) said yesterday.

The labor market is expected to remain stable, with unemployment likely to decline further this month and next month, the agency said.

The unemployment rate edged down to 3.35 percent, 0.01 percentage points lower than September and a year earlier, the lowest October reading since 2000. After seasonal adjustments, the rate was unchanged from September at 3.33 percent.

“The labor market remained stable amid favorable economic conditions, and the unemployment rate is likely to continue its seasonal decline over the final two months of the year,” Census Department Deputy Director Tan Wen-ling (譚文玲) told a news conference in Taipei.

The labor force participation rate rose to 59.63 percent last month, its highest level in almost 37 years, as more women and older people entered the workforce amid government efforts toward their inclusion, Tan said.

However, Taiwan’s persistently low birthrate poses a longer-term challenge to labor supply as the working-age population continues to shrink, she said.

The number of unemployed people fell by 1,000, or 0.22 percent, to 404,000, as a 3,000 decline in first-time jobseekers more than offset a 2,000 increase in people who had left their previous jobs, DGBAS data showed.

University graduates had the highest unemployment rate among education groups, at 4.45 percent, followed by people with postgraduate degrees at 3.13 percent and those with senior-high school or vocational-high school qualifications at 3.08 percent, the data showed.

Younger workers continued to face greater challenges entering the job market, as the unemployment rate among people aged 15 to 24 stood at 11.46 percent, largely reflecting first-time job searches and difficulties adjusting to workplace requirements, the DGBAS said. The rate was 5.75 percent among those aged 25 to 29 and 3.45 percent among those aged 30 to 34.

Despite the overall improvement, the average duration of unemployment lengthened by 1.4 weeks to 20.3 weeks last month, the agency said.

The number of people who had been unemployed for at least a year rose by 3,000 from the previous month to 45,000, unchanged from a year earlier, it said.

Taiwan’s seasonally adjusted unemployment rate of 3.33 percent remained relatively high compared with other Asian economies, including Singapore at 3 percent, South Korea at 2.5 percent and Japan at 2.4 percent, the DGBAS said.

data.title: Precision stamping should drive sales, Shieh Yih says
data.description:
BUSINESS TREND: The company said that Asia has been its strongest market this year due to growing automotive and AI server investments in Southeast Asia

Servo stamping press maker Shieh Yih Machinery Industry Co (協易機) expects tighter artificial intelligence (AI) rack layouts and improved cold-plate manufacturing processes to drive demand for high-precision, leak-proof server rack structures and thinner slide rails, benefiting the company next year.

As servers require greater structural strength and cooling performance, suppliers are adopting new materials and more precise forming technologies, driving demand for stamping equipment, Shieh Yih president Steven Lee (李承偉) said during an earnings conference in Taipei yesterday.

The company manufactures metal stamping presses used to produce components for cars, servers, home appliances and other industrial applications. Its customers include Chenbro Micom Co (勤誠), King Slide Works Co (川湖), Auras Technology Co (雙鴻) and Asia Vital Components Co (奇鋐), Lee said.

Shieh Yih is developing a new high-rigidity, high-precision plate forging press, the SK1, for forming ultra-thin and high-strength metals, which is scheduled to enter mass production in the first quarter of next year, he said.

The machine can reduce stamping deformation to about 0.03mm, compared with 0.1mm to 0.12mm for conventional equipment, improving precision and reducing subsequent reshaping processes, with applications including casings, slide rails, cooling components and fuel-cell bipolar plates, he said.

The company sees the SK1 as an important growth driver next year, he added.

The company reported third-quarter revenue rose 14.74 percent quarter-on-quarter and 14.09 percent year-on-year to NT$1.19 billion (US$36.18 million). Net profit was NT$47.87 million in the third quarter, compared with a net loss of NT$10.77 million in the previous quarter, but down 3.77 percent year-on-year, with earnings per share of NT$0.27.

Asia has been Shieh Yih’s strongest market this year due to growing automotive and AI server-related investments in Southeast Asia, Lee said.

The Chinese market continues to grow despite intense competition, while the US and European markets have been weaker due to inflation, policy uncertainty and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, he said.

Shieh Yih foresees no significant changes in US orders or projects following the midterm elections and expects US data center demand to remain strong next year, with the end market potentially growing more than 30 percent, and supporting Asian component and equipment suppliers, he added.

data.title: Market correction manageable: SinoPac
data.description:
SinoPac Financial Holdings Co (永豐金控) yesterday said that a global stock market correction would weigh on its earnings this quarter, particularly trading and fee income, but the impact should remain manageable, as most of this year’s earnings have already been secured.

The financial holding company made the assessment after reporting record earnings for the first three quarters, driven by broad-based growth across its core businesses, even as a correction in technology stocks at home and abroad clouded the near-term outlook.

Net income jumped 79 percent year-on-year to a record NT$36.86 billion (US$1.12 billion) in the first three quarters, with earnings per share reaching NT$2.49.

Lower funding costs and an expanding loan book lifted net interest income 41 percent, while stronger wealth management and securities brokerage businesses boosted net fee income 68 percent. Other net income rose 49 percent, reflecting brisk capital market activity and stronger gains from proprietary trading and venture capital investments, SinoPac Financial president Stanley Chu (朱士廷) told a news conference in Taipei.

The company expects the central bank to raise interest rates by 12.5 basis points next month and again in March next year, while the US Federal Reserve might deliver three 25-basis-point increases next month, and in January and March next year, Chu said.

Higher interest rates would benefit financial companies, but a decline in stock market turnover could dampen investor sentiment and weigh on brokerage and other market-related income, SinoPac Financial chief financial officer Kerry Hsu (許如玫) said.

Waning confidence in the artificial intelligence outlook is the biggest source of uncertainty for Taiwan’s stock market, SinoPac Securities Co (永豐金證券) president William Su (蘇威嘉) said.

Trading volume this quarter is expected to fall 10 percent from the previous quarter, putting pressure on brokerage revenue, Su said.

The TAIEX had previously been expected to reach the 45,000 to 50,000-point range toward the end of this year, but that milestone now appears more likely to be reached in the first or second quarter of next year, he said.

Average daily trading volume next year might be slightly below this year’s average of about NT$1.2 trillion, partly reflecting this year’s unusually active market, but should remain above the NT$1 trillion level, Su forecast.

SinoPac Securities would fully cooperate with measures proposed by the Financial Supervisory Commission to stabilize the market, including easing restrictions on securities lending and margin maintenance requirements, Su added.

The TAIEX tends to move in tandem with the US Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, also known as the SOX Index, Chu said.

The SOX Index’s forward price-to-earnings ratio for next year has fallen to about 12 times, below its historical range of 15 to 24 times, suggesting that semiconductor stocks have become relatively attractive, he said.

“Investors should stay rational during rallies and remain calm during downturns,” Chu said.

data.title: AI boom drives hiring demand beyond tech sector: Report
data.description:
Artificial intelligence (AI) development is driving demand for talent beyond the technology sector, with job openings in chemical-related manufacturing surging more than 70 percent in the third quarter from the first quarter, a report jointly released yesterday by the Institute for Information Industry (III) and online job bank 1111 showed.

The report showed that job openings in the chemical industry, whose manufacturers supply materials such as glass cloth and copper-clad laminate (CCL) used in AI-related products, increased 74.32 percent in the third quarter compared with the first quarter, the highest growth among major industries in Taiwan.

The warehousing and transportation support services sector also benefited from AI-related business expansion, recording the second-largest increase in AI-related job openings at 44.83 percent, followed by the architectural planning and design industry, which saw a 24.57 percent increase, the report said.

“Demand for AI talent is no longer limited to the technology industry,” the report said. “As various industries accelerate their digital transformation, demand for AI and information technology talent is growing simultaneously.”

In the technology sector, job openings in computer and consumer electronics manufacturing increased 23.26 percent in the third quarter from the first quarter, while the electronics components and semiconductor industries recorded increases of 18.61 percent and 13.63 percent respectively, the report showed.

III deputy executive director Lin Yu-fan (林玉凡) said in the report that as the AI era unfolds, workers will need to develop four key qualities, which she described as the four “I”s: “Imagination,” “Integration,” “Impact” and “Investment.”

“Imagination” refers to identifying innovative opportunities to apply AI in the workplace and across industries, while “Integration” means connecting technology, data, processes and on-site requirements across different fields, Lin said.

“Impact” involves creating value through internal and external communication, while “Investment” refers to continuous learning and practical experience to keep pace with technological advances and changes in the workplace, she added.

Lin also predicted that positions related to AI agents will be in high demand.

She said people working in the field should begin with small-scale applications, accurately identify pain points and quickly put the technology into practice to build up successful cases. Otherwise, they could encounter problems involving insufficient data, security risks and inadequate processes, she added.

According to the report, job openings for AI-related engineers increased 66.12 percent in the third quarter compared with the first quarter, while openings for algorithm development engineers rose 54.41 percent. Cybersecurity engineers and systems engineers also saw increases of 35.47 percent and 26.38 percent, respectively.

Enditem/ASG

data.title: Margin calls soared 200-fold in Taiwan as traders fled AI bets
data.description:
Taiwan’s stock market plunged almost 18 percent last week, its worst selloff since 1991. That sent brokers and investors rushing for cover. Margin calls hit NT$6.46 billion (US$196 million) on Friday, more than 200 times the volume just a month before, according to data from the Taiwan Stock Exchange (TWSE). Regulators curbed short selling, and called a weekend meeting with brokers to discuss other steps.

Authorities were desperately trying to stop the rout turning into a prolonged crash. After margin loans tumbled US$1.5 billion on Friday, a record decline according to data going back to 1996, around US$13 billion remained outstanding. That suggests there is still some appetite to hold stocks — but it also creates a path for share prices to tumble further.

In an effort to stem the slide, officials have unleashed the NT$500 billion (US$15.2 billion) National Stabilization Fund (NSF). The fund appeared to intervene in the market multiple times yesterday, squeezing foreign short sellers by loading up on stocks during morning trading, Fubon Securities Investment Services Co (富邦投顧) chairman Edward Chen (陳奕光) said.

That helped the benchmark TAIEX rise just over 2 percent yesterday. But analysts say the state fund’s buying alone won’t be enough to shift sentiment in the battered stock market.

The selloff in Taiwan is a dramatic reversal for a market that has become one of the great winners of the artificial intelligence (AI) trade. It is also a reminder of how far the panic around AI is rippling through global markets, raising questions about a sector that in just a few years has gone from an academic curiosity to a driving force of market sentiment.

“What’s happening in Taiwan’s market right now could be the biggest test yet of investor confidence in the AI trade,” Allspring Global Investments Holdings LLC fund manager Gary Tan (譚頌超) said in Singapore. “Taiwan is one of the most AI-exposed benchmarks and has been one of the biggest beneficiaries from the AI boom.”

The pain of Taiwan’s stock market selloff has been exacerbated by a dip-buying mentality among local investors, who have largely been rewarded this year for keeping their faith in the stock market even during times of turmoil. These investors are now learning the hard way that dips can sometimes turn into routs.

AI Reckoning

The selloff in Taiwan was part of a broader reckoning for the AI trade, which roiled global markets last week. Chinese tech stocks capped a US$1.7 trillion market value decline since the end of June. The NASDAQ 100 index fell 5.6 percent on Friday to cement its worst week since March 2020. From Europe to the Americas, most major stock indexes joined the downturn.

But Taiwan is almost uniquely reliant on optimism around AI. The island of around 23 million people has become a crucial part of the tech supply chain. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電), the giant chipmaker that boasts Nvidia Corp. among its clients, makes up over 40 percent of the benchmark TAIEX alone.

That meant that when fears around AI spread through global stock markets, following the shock ouster of Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) from Nvidia and the Democrats’ decisive victory in the US midterm elections, Taiwan was particularly vulnerable. TSMC’s shares fell 15 percent last week. Investors quickly moved to cut their exposure to the wider market.

Wealthy investors with positions worth more than US$30 million aggressively dumped stocks, according to people familiar with the matter. Many young traders who made their fortunes in recent years as tech stocks boomed were willing to sell at any price, the people said.

Foreign investors were already pulling out even before the recent selloff. They net sold a record US$30 billion of Taiwanese stocks last month, and have already cut more than US$25 billion so far this month, according to Bloomberg-compiled data. That meant there was less liquidity in the market to compensate for the pullback from retail investors.

Taiwanese officials unleashed an arsenal of measures to bring an end to the market rout. The Financial Supervisory Commission tightened short-selling curbs yet again on Saturday, banning such trades below the previous day’s close across the market after two earlier rounds of restrictions failed to stop the slide. It also raised the minimum margin requirement for short sales to 150 percent from 130 percent.

TWSE officials met executives from the island’s 10 largest brokerages over the weekend to discuss additional measures to support the market, including cutting margin requirements. The move was officially announced yesterday.

The NSF also tried to calm nerves. In a statement over the weekend, the fund said it had been buying stocks since Nov. 6. It urged investors to remain confident in Taiwan’s stock market, pointing to earnings growth and strong economic fundamentals.

Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) said yesterday the government will consider expanding the fund amid concerns that its current firepower may be insufficient to steady markets during bouts of turmoil.

For now, though, investors don’t appear convinced. Their faith in the AI trade has finally been shaken — and even committed dip-buyers are hoarding cash.

data.title: No new curbs on Nvidia chips
data.description:
CHINA LEANING? The US has greenlit the sale of less-than-cutting-edge Nvidia chips to China, amidst national security and technology control concerns

US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent said on Friday that no more restrictions on the sale of older Nvidia Corp chips to China were needed following US President Donald Trump administration’s move earlier last week to block China’s remote access to the latest semiconductors.

The ability of Chinese tech firms to access Nvidia’s technology came under scrutiny after CEO Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) stepped down amid allegations of his affair with an executive at Megaspeed International Pte Ltd, a Singapore-based company that uses advanced chips to generate computing power that Chinese firms access remotely.

“The proper chip restrictions are in place,” Bessent said in an interview after returning from a trip to Asia with Trump. “And the remote access has been curtailed.”

Bessent’s comments came a day after the House Foreign Affairs Committee released details of the US Department of Commerce’s approval of the sales of more than 850,000 chips from Nvidia and its competitor Advanced Micro Devices Inc (AMD) to Chinese companies. The Pentagon has said that some of those companies have ties to the Chinese military.

The report tracked applications from Nvidia to sell its H200 chips — one of its more powerful products, though not the most advanced — and AMD’s applications to sell its roughly comparable MI325X chip to companies that are either located or headquartered in China, or entities with parent companies based in China.

The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) approved the export, re-export, or transfer of 879,868 of these chips to companies with Chinese ties across 21 license applications as of May 11, the report said. Nvidia and AMD had requested to sell more than 3.4 million of the chips to Chinese-tied companies across those applications, per the report.

The approvals, which do not necessarily indicate completed sales, included 75,000 for Alibaba Group Holding Ltd (阿里巴巴), 150,000 for Tencent Holdings Ltd (騰訊) and its subsidiaries, 43,000 for Baidu Inc (百度) and 4,000 for BYD Co (比亞迪), according to the report. Each of those companies has been identified by the US Department of Defense as having ties to the Chinese military.

An Nvidia spokesperson said in a statement on Friday that the “limited shipments we made under the H200 program were legal and authorized” by the BIS. “The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes,” the company spokesperson said.

Earlier last week, Nvidia said it was no longer shipping H200 chips to China. The spokesperson said on Friday that shipments had stopped despite prior approvals.

AMD said it complies with US export control laws and regulations and maintains “rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations” in a statement from a spokesperson on Friday. “We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity,” the spokesperson said.

Separately, US securities regulators are investigating the accounting practices of Nvidia, according to US media.

The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) inquiry is in its early stages, The New York Times reported on Saturday, citing people briefed on the confidential investigation.

The Wall Street Journal reported on the investigation earlier last week, although it was unable to establish its precise focus. The probe could end without any charges being brought against the company.

Nvidia last year changed how it reported sales by geographical location, switching from customers’ billing addresses to the countries where they are headquartered, US media reported.

The change removed Singapore from its geographical breakdown, despite the company’s significant business there.

It remains unclear whether the SEC investigation is connected to those accounting changes or to the scandal surrounding Huang.

Additional reporting by AFP

data.title: Export boom sends Q3 surplus soaring
data.description:
BOOM DRIVEN: The third-quarter current account surplus was the second-highest on record, well up from last year, and lagging only behind last year’s fourth quarter

Taiwan’s current account surplus in the third quarter of this year reached its second-highest level on record, as exports hit new highs on the back of robust global demand for artificial intelligence (AI)-related applications, the central bank said on Friday.

The surplus rose by US$22.04 billion from a year earlier to US$68.79 billion in the third quarter, second only to the US$69.69 billion recorded in the fourth quarter of last year, the bank said.

The current account mainly measures a country’s transactions in goods and services, as well as primary and secondary income flows with the rest of the world.

Taiwan’s merchandise trade surplus hit a record US$70.95 billion in the third quarter, up US $20.94 billion from a year earlier, as the country benefited from the growing demand for emerging technologies, including AI-related devices, the bank said.

Taiwan’s exports continued to set new records, reaching US$225.8 billion in the three-month period, it said.

In the services account, the third quarter is traditionally the peak season for tourism, as Taiwanese people tend to travel overseas during summer vacation, the bank said.

This pushed outbound travel spending to a record US $6.87 billion in the quarter, while travel receipts from foreign visitors hit US$2.638 billion, it said.

After deducting travel receipts, net travel expenditures reached US$4.233 billion, a record high for a single quarter, the bank said.

The central bank said the merchandise trade surplus was the main source of Taiwan’s current account surplus. It added that whether Taiwanese exporters repatriate their overseas sales proceeds or retain the funds abroad, their overseas sales contribute to an increase in Taiwan’s net foreign assets.

In the third quarter, Taiwan recorded a net financial account outflow of US$62.21 billion, up US$24.79 billion from a year earlier, the 65th consecutive quarter of net outflows, the bank said.

During the three-month period, Taiwan’s direct investment account posted a net increase in assets of US$11.20 billion, it said.

Outward direct investment by Taiwanese residents and inward direct investment by nonresidents recorded net increases of US$15.51 billion and US$4.31 billion, respectively, it added.

Department of Economic Research Deputy Director Tsai Mei-fen (蔡美芬) said the increase in outward direct investment reflected efforts by major Taiwanese technology companies to expand their global operations, while investments by foreign high-tech companies and offshore wind power developers contributed to the increase in inward direct investment.

Addressing concerns that investors would continue moving funds out of the country and into US dollar-denominated assets, the central bank said net financial account outflows were common among economies such as Taiwan that have maintained long-term current account surpluses.

Other economies with persistent current account surpluses, such as Japan, South Korea, Singapore and Germany, have recorded net financial account outflows, the bank said.
